newsitem.title: CROATIA: Technical problems mar Croatian local elections.
newsitem.headline: Technical problems mar Croatian local elections.

text.p: Croatian elections intended to convince Serbs in east Slavonia they will be safe when the former rebel enclave shortly returns to Zagreb's rule began amid chaos and anger on Sunday.

The nationwide elections for municipal and county authorities were also a test for President Franjo Tudjman's ruling HDZ party which has become increasingly unpopular despite having led Croatia to independence from former Yugoslavia.

Tudjman's government is under strong international pressure to create conditions acceptable to the 150,000 Serbs of east Slavonia and prevent them fleeing in fear of vengeance from returning Croat refugees.

The U.N.-supervised vote in east Slavonia was supposed to be a model of efficient organisation after heavily criticised elections run in Bosnia last year by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).
But it quickly unravelled with some voting stations opening late, ballot papers going astray and registration lists found incomplete.
General Jacques Klein, head of the U.N. transitional administration (UNTAES) in east Slavonia tried to soothe angry ethnic Serb leaders with the possibility of voting being extended into Monday.
"That is an option. We will look into that this afternoon. I will not disenfranchise anyone," he told reporters.
The polling stations across the country were supposed to have opened at 7 a.m., but by 9.30 a.m. only around 100 out of 171 voting stations in Eastern Slavonia were operating.
Reuters reporters in the village of Pacetin saw local Serbs crowding in front of a school from the early morning, only to be told to come later as voting materials had not arrived.

"Everybody should have been voting by now, but things are way beyond my control. I am very disgusted, very disappointed with what is going on," David Costanza, a local U.N. field electoral officer said.
U.N. spokesman Philip Arnold said the problems were mainly technical, ruling out any notion that they were a deliberate attempt to obstruct the elections.
"There were some logistical problems. We had mismatched ballot packages, some of which were delivered to wrong places," he told Reuters.
The confusion was compounded by late Serb requests for Croatian documents which led to last-minute revisions of voting lists.
Vojislav Stanimirovic, the Serb leader of the region said that the elections were irregular, but supported Klein's efforts to rectify the situation.
"Unfortunately there are more irregularities going on than regularities," Stanimirovic said, appealing to all Serbs to wait for the problems to be dealt with "in dignity and not allow any incident".

People possessing Croatian documents are missing from lists, whole streets have not been entered, elections materials were not in place and over 3,500 people have left stations after waiting for two hours, a statement from Serb parties said.
In the rest of the country, the poll seemed to be going on as planned. Croatian President Franjo Tudjman cast his ballot in the wealthy Zagreb area of Tuskanac, where he lives.
The HDZ is tipped to win in smaller and rural municipalities but are likely to lose the big urban centres, including the capital Zagreb, to the centre-left opposition.
In a refugee camp in Cepin near Osijek, some two thirds of 2,600 Croatian refugees have already voted by 10 a.m., and most of those interviewed by Reuters said they were voting for HDZ.

"The HDZ is the only party which can keep people together and later we shall see. All the other parties have been promising a lot, but the HDZ is the only one which have already achieved something," said refugee Darko Valentic, 30.
Thousands of Croatian refugees are due to return to Eastern Slavonia, from where they were expelled in the 1991-95 war, when the area comes under Zagreb's rule in mid July.
Many local Serbs are thought to be planning to leave by then despite Croatian government security guarantees, and some were leaving even as the elections were starting.
Earlier on Sunday, reporters saw six Serb families packed with all their belongings on tractors, heading from Eastern Slavonia in the direction of Serb-led Yugoslavia.
"If I wanted to live under the (Croatian) checkered flag I would have accepted it peacefully five years ago," an elderly Serb said, referring to the Croatian coat of arms.
